Question: Why are distorted human faces, with big round eyes and showing teeth or with a strange expression, more frightening than other frightening things?
Answer: This is a surprisingly deep and subtle question, and a lot of research has gone into it. First of all, yes, it is absolutely true, we do seem disposed to finding distorted human figures and faces particularly distressing. I seem to recall this is also true for other primates as well—that experiments with chimps and bonobos show they react with fear to distorted pictures of chimps and bonobos. It even has a name, the “uncanny valley effect.” Cartoon distortions of human figures look cute to us, but as they get more and more realistic they suddenly hit a point where they become disgusting, frightening, or disturbing. The main hypothesis as far as I know (mind you, this is from my cog sci class in my uni days, so it may be out of date) is disease. Many diseases—end stage syphilis, leprosy, smallpox, and so on—disfigure their victims. People with an aversion to distorted or disfigured people avoided them, so were less likely to die of communicable disease. A predisposition to being afraid of disfigured humans—nearly but not quite human-looking—had positive survival value.

Question: Why do we believe that whatever a writer portrays in their work is what they like or believe in?
Answer: Hmm. “Like or believe in” is doing some pretty heavy lifting there. Writer here. I make my living writing novels. The things you’ll find in my novels often are things I like and believe in… …but just as often they’re things that worry or horrify me. My co-author Eunice was at WorldCon with a big pile of our books recently. One of the novels she has with her was immechanica, our near-future, hard-SF dystopia. This is definitely not a world we like and believe in. We extrapolated from real-world tech, political, social, and environmental trends to try to create a worst-case scenario. Our goal was to write a warning, something we feared, not something we liked. And a really fucked-up thing happened at WorldCon. So there’s a passage in immechanica that goes like this: Safan slid a small black case across the table to her. It reminded Nadine a bit of something an engagement ring might come in, about the same width but three times longer. She snapped it open. Inside lay a thing like a mechanical wasp, smooth glossy black, with thin wings of some clear plastic. The front was pointed, with two lenses that suggested eyes. Overall, it had a sleek, menacing look that made Nadine’s skin crawl. “What is it?” “Swarm drone. A bunch of these will follow you in, all controlled remotely. Anyone turns up to give you grief, well…” A nasty grin crossed his face. “You designate a threat. The swarm picks the closest drone, it locks on, fires a propulsive charge, tears into the target and then explodes. Core is a foot of grooved tungsten wire dipped in wax impregnated with quick-acting nerve agent, wrapped around half a gram of crystallized high explosive.” “Jesus.” Nadine dropped the case on the table. “Who comes up with shit like this?” Someone stopped by the Luminastra Press booth at the con to say “yeah, my company is working on explosive micro-drone weapons, how did you know?” When she told me, I was like “Jesus Christ on a tap-dancing camel, immechanica was supposed to be a warning, not a goddamn how-to guide!” Fuck me dead, we weren’t dark enough. So yeah, if you read immechanica and come away with “oh, look, this is what these authors like and believe in,” either we have failed in our role as writers or you need psychiatric help immediately. Now, that said, yes, a lot of our novels do describe things we like and believe in. The Passionate Pantheon novels, set in a far-future, post-scarcity society with virtually limitless radical longevity and strong AI, describe a place we would both like to live. The novels are written as pornography, so of course there’s tons and tons and oodles and tons of really kinky, highly explicit sex…but we use the sex to explore philosophy, meaning, community, accountability, and a bunch of other things we both care passionately about. We also explore ways a utopian post-scarcity society can go wrong. The odd-numbered novels in the series are upbeat utopias; the even-numbered novels are erotic horror, where we take the themes in the odd-numbered books and invert them. We even have a blog where we talk about the philosophical themes in the novels, though we haven’t had time to update it since Eunice started working on her postgraduate degree. So is that a series where we talk about things we like and believe in? Yes, but we also talk about ways it can become problematic, too.

Question: How do you write your non-fiction e-book for Kindle? Do you use Notepad, MS Word, OpenOffice, Google Docs, or another tool before importing it into Kindle Create? Do you use the "native" styles (title, subtitle, etc.) or a customized template?
Answer: When I write, I use Google Docs. The book is not published, in print or in ebook, from a Docs file, though. Instead, after editing, the manuscript is laid out in Adobe InDesign. The InDesign file is sent to the printer as a PDF (well, actually two, one for the cover and one for the interior), then exported as an ePub which is brought into Calibre for fine-tuning and cleanup. How I write: How the book is laid out: How the eBook is laid out: The Google Docs file is exported to Word to be brought into InDesign, but all the Word styles are stripped out and instead the various elements of the book are assigned styles created specifically for that book in InDesign. You can see the Styles palette in the second screenshot. The InDesign styles are set up for both print and ePub, and in particular the “Split Book for ePub” style is used for chapter headers and anything else that must start on a new page, so that the ePub breaks into chapters correctly. (This is something novices frequently fall afoul of; setting up styles with an eye toward how they’ll be used in the ePub, and particularly where the internal ePub files will split, is absolutely crucial.) No professional publishing workflow uses Word files directly, for print or eBook publishing. The manuscript might be given to the publisher in Word format, but the Word file is placed in a page layout app. These days that’s almost always InDesign, though some folks still use QuarkXPress and a tiny handful cling to Frame Maker. (LaTeX markup is occasionally used in niche publishing, like for math textbooks.) This workflow (word processor of some sort, be that Docs or Scrivener or Word or whatever -> InDesign -> eBook editor like Calibre or Sigil) is pretty typical in the publishing industry. Outside of textbooks, it probably accounts for 80% of all the books professionally published.

Question: Why is the re-entry point of the Earth's atmosphere so hot from the space that space crafts need heat shields to survive burning?
Answer: Compressive heating. When you take a gas, any gas, and compress it, it gets hotter. When you take a gas and release the pressure, it gets colder. This is how air conditioners and heat pumps work. A spacecraft in orbit has to travel at around 17,000 miles an hour, or roughly 29,000 kilometers per hour for those of you who use reasonable measurements. That’s really fast, the equivalent of about Mach 22 at sea level. At that speed, way way faster than sound, air literally cannot get out of the way of the re-entering spacecraft fast enough, so it gets ferociously compressed, and that means it gets ferociously hot.
